claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are controlled by surface chemical segregation.
During heating, Cu preferentially diffuses to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation produces a chemically distinct, Cu-enriched shell.
The segregated shell premelts at a lower temperature than the uniformly mixed core.
The starting Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are equiatomic and chemically homogeneous.
The starting nanoparticles possess a solid-solution structure.
A thermal annealing pretreatment can promote surface segregation relative to the as-synthesized state.
The controlled comparison uses annealed and untreated Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Development of a Cu-enriched surface layer reduces the local melting point at the nanoparticle surface.
Cu enrichment modifies local cohesive energy.
The modified local cohesive energy makes the outer shell thermally unstable at a lower temperature than the core.
Nanoparticles retaining uniform composition have a higher and more spatially uniform onset of premelting.
Annealed nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will exhibit earlier surface-premelting onset than untreated, uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
Uniform baseline nanoparticles will show less pronounced surface–core differences during melting.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles approximately 10–50 nm in size under high-vacuum or inert atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially larger particles.
Oxidizing conditions may limit applicability by introducing additional surface reactions.
Internal lattice strain and nanoscale confinement may also influence melting behavior.
Premelting onset, melting progression, heat-flow signatures, and elemental distributions can be compared using in situ TEM, DSC, and EDS.
Statistically similar premelting onset temperatures and melting behavior in verified segregated and uniform particles would falsify the proposed governing role of surface segregation.
